definition: Stagnant means still to the point of going stale — not flowing, not moving, not developing.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word stagnant. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know stagnant should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: By August the attic office turned stagnant — no vent, no fan, the same warm air hanging over the desks from morning to night.
Sluggish is weaker than stagnant — a sluggish stream still creeps forward, while a stagnant one has stopped moving entirely and begun to sour.
Putrid is stronger than stagnant — stagnant water is stale from standing still, but putrid water has finished the job and rotted outright.
simply not moving — a parked car, a held breath. Stagnant adds the sourness of it: stillness that has lasted long enough to begin going stale.
still moving, just heavily and slowly — sluggish traffic crawls, a sluggish stream creeps. Stagnant goes further: the movement has stopped altogether.
unreactive — failing to respond or act when something touches it, the way inert gases sit out every reaction. Stagnant blames the stillness itself and watches the decay that follows it.
moving along in a steady current
growing strongly and healthily

Latin stagnum built almost nothing else in English, but its small family is busy: economists borrowed the same standing pool for stagnation — a stretch in which wages, prices, and output all sit as still as the water that named them.
Stagnant means still to the point of going stale — not flowing, not moving, not developing.
Three years into the job, Marisol admitted her career had gone stagnant: the same title, the same tasks, and a skills list she had not added to since her training week.

The word begins at the pond's edge — water that stops flowing soon clouds and sours — and English carries the picture to anything that stops moving and starts to stale: careers, wages, whole economies.
Stagnant is not merely slow; it asserts that motion has stopped entirely, and that the standstill has begun to do damage.
neutral, mildly disapproving — reporting, science, and business writing
Stagnant always carries a verdict: the stillness has lasted too long and something is spoiling for it.
A pond can be still and lovely; call it stagnant and you have said it has begun to sour.
The same charge rides along in figurative use — stagnant wages, a stagnant career — where the word asserts both that growth has stopped and that the standing still is doing harm.
motionless: simply not moving — a parked car, a held breath.
Stagnant adds the sourness of it: stillness that has lasted long enough to begin going stale.
sluggish: still moving, just heavily and slowly — sluggish traffic crawls, a sluggish stream creeps.

inert: unreactive — failing to respond or act when something touches it, the way inert gases sit out every reaction.
